rows.description: A mature reader treats a wince, grin or scowl as one clue among tone, words and situation, holding the guess loosely and checking with the person, because the same face can come from several different states.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young professional keeps a pleasant face with clients or a manager during a stressful day, which is useful, but long-term suppression can be tiring and is best balanced with honest outlets elsewhere.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Broad smile as customer or leadership tool [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional uses a broad, open-mouth smile to set clients at ease or to open a meeting. It works best when it matches honest goodwill, and habitual smiling over real worry can wear a person down.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Sustained smile in intimacy and grief [Mismatch]
rows.description: A sustained smile can appear at reunions, weddings or even a funeral when remembering a loved one, mixing joy with sorrow. Readers should not assume a smile means only happiness.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: joy, affection, sadness, grief

rows.description: A young adult flashes the eyebrows to acknowledge a colleague across a room, a light signal of recognition and friendliness. It is easy to overlook, so it complements rather than replaces a greeting.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A colleague's habitually drawn-together brows may reflect worry, concentration, headaches or simply how the face rests. Asking kindly about workload is wiser than reading a mood into a resting brow.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Wet or squeezed eyes under pressure [Regulating]
rows.description: An adult blinks quickly, squeezes the eyes or looks up to hold back tears at work, a common way to regulate strong feeling. A short break to breathe often helps more.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: relief from stress

rows.subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional widens the eyes slightly to show interest and encourage a speaker. It works when natural, and a fixed wide-eyed look may seem strained.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young professional working across countries learns that gaze norms vary: sustained eye contact means engagement in some places and challenge in others. Adapting while staying curious avoids stereotypes.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
rows.description: A colleague glancing down at a phone during a talk may signal boredom, urgency or an actual work task. Naming the concern and asking for full attention is kinder than assuming disrespect.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
